strengths: The paper addresses an identifiable audience interested in high-dimensional classification with dense, spiked covariance matrices. Selecting coordinates after whitening provides a useful perspective distinct from sparsity of the original discriminant direction.
The use of bounded coherence and entrywise eigenvector perturbation bounds offers a promising framework for analyzing whitening and support recovery without assuming bounded leading eigenvalues.

Explicit algorithms, assumptions, and substantial proof appendices make the approach understandable. The experimental design includes relevant baselines, several covariance structures, 200 Monte Carlo replications with standard deviations, and two gene-expression datasets.
weaknesses: Necessary correction—QDA consistency is false under the stated conditions. Equation (5.9) does not follow from (5.7): sparse whitened means do not imply that covariance-based discrimination is confined to their supports. For example, take equal priors, u = 1/sqrt(p), Σ1 = I + p uuᵀ, Σ2 = 4Σ1, and µ1 = µ2 = Σ1^(1/2)e1. These satisfy the stated QDA sparsity, spike, and coherence conditions, with whitened means e1 and e1/2. Algorithm 4 retains only coordinate 1. Even with known parameters and an optimal threshold, its error is approximately 0.339, whereas the full Bayes error tends to zero by distinguishing the classes through their total squared radius. Estimating the threshold cannot restore the discarded information. Theorem 6 therefore requires a substantive redesign, additional structural restrictions, or removal.

Necessary correction—the main LDA theorem exceeds what its proof establishes. Theorem 3 claims almost-sure convergence of conditional risk under log(p) = o(n), but Section 8.4 concludes convergence in probability of the discriminant score under the stronger condition log(n)log(p) = o(n). The bound in (8.47) need not vanish under the theorem's stated condition. The proof also does not establish the claimed almost-sure conditional-risk conclusion from this joint convergence in probability. Repair these steps or narrow the theorem and corresponding abstract and conclusion claims.

Necessary correction—the elliptical extension overstates Bayes optimality. For a common elliptical radial density h and unequal class priors, the likelihood ratio contains log h(r1) − log h(r2), which generally is not the Gaussian linear score with a log-prior adjustment. Monotonicity and sub-Gaussian tails do not establish the claimed equivalence. Sections 5.1–5.2 need restrictions such as equal priors and a common radial density, or a suitable likelihood-based classifier and analysis.

Necessary verification—the reported oracle errors contradict the specified simulation models. Applying Equation (3.1) to Model 2 at ρ = 0.9 gives approximately 0.0196% Bayes error, whereas Table 3 reports 5.40%. For Model 1 at ρ = 0.8, the corresponding value is approximately 0.0221%, whereas Table 1 reports 0.19%. These discrepancies are much larger than the stated Monte Carlo uncertainty; several entries also repeat between the ρ = 0.7 and 0.8 columns. Reconcile the data-generation specifications, implementations, and tables before relying on the empirical comparisons.

Necessary clarification—the model-size advantage compares different quantities. Although Section 2.2 distinguishes whitened and original coordinates, the headline comparisons count retained whitened coordinates for the proposed method and original coefficients for methods such as DSDA. A dense whitening matrix generally requires all original measurements even when only a few transformed coordinates are retained. The gene-expression results therefore support compact transformed representations, not necessarily fewer measured genes; the feature-selection claims should maintain this distinction.

Optional improvements—add a simulation satisfying all theoretical assumptions while varying n and p, and examine sensitivity to the 90% explained-variance rule for choosing d. This would connect the fixed-spike analysis more directly to the practical implementation. These improvements are secondary to the mathematical and numerical correctness issues above, which substantively prevent the current manuscript from satisfying the evidence criterion.
